full_judgment:
Respondent .No. 1 brought the writ petition on the averment, inter alia, that three full brothers; namely, Noor Hossain, Mosharraf Hossain and Tozammal Hossain and one Saghir Ahmed initially formed a partnership firm under the name and style of Messrs East Pakistan, Rubber Industries in terms of an  agreement of a partnership dated 7-5-1957 (that' another brother Iqbal Hussain was admitted to the said partnership as a minor). The Government of erstwhile East Pakistan allotted a piece of land measuring 1 (one) acre appertaining to an industrial Plot No. 278 at Tejgaon Industrial Area, Dhaka in the name of the said partnership firm on 26-8-1960. the partner, Noor Hussain died on 23-7-1968 leaving behind his two sons, namely, Anwar Husain and Iftekhar Husain, four daughters, Jinnat Husain (Zinat Husain), Jesmin Husain (minor), Israt Husain (minor)! Sharmin Husain (mitior), a widow Rowshan Ara Hussain and mother Zohra Khatun. They became partners of the said firm as Noor Hossain's legal heirs. Meanwhile, minor Iqbal Husain having attained majority became a full-fledged partner along with others under a reconstituted deed of partnership dated 24-7-1968. A standard lease deed for a period of 99 years in respect of the said industrial plot was executed on 20-1-1970 and registered on 17-2-1971 between the Government of erstwhile East Pakistan and the said partnership firm. On 31-8-1970, another partner Mosharaf Husain resigned from the partnership business in term of a compromise decree passed in Title Suit No. 65 of 1970 in the third Court of the then learned Subordinate Judge, Dhaka. After liberation war, the name of the firm was changed as 'Bangladesh Rubber Industries by a deed of rectification. In consequence thereof the change was, recorded with the Registrar of Firms. Thereafter, a deed of agreement for dissolution of the firm was executed on 31-12-1975 by the remaining partners, namely, Mrs. Rawshan Ara Hossain, Mr Iftekhar Hussain, Mr Anwar Hossain and Miss Zeenat Hossain (heirs of late Noor Hossain) on the one hand and Mr Tofazammel Hossain, Mr Iqbal Hossain, Mrs. Zohra Khatun and Mr Sagir Ahmed, on the other hand, vide Annexure-D under the terms and conditions stated therein. After dissolution of the aforesaid partnership, late Noor Hossain's heirs, namely, Anwar Hussain and Iftekhar Husain, four daughters, Zinat Hussain, Jesmin Hussain (minor), Ishrat Hussain (minor) and Sharmin Hussain (minor) and widow Rowshan Ara Hussain, executed a fresh partnership deed dated 1-1-1976 (admitting the minors to, the benefit of partnership) to run and continue a partnership business vide Annexure-E and they got it registered with the Registrar of Joint Stock Companies and Firms under the Partnership Act being Registration No.PF/22285 (wrongly written PR 33385) dated 9-11-1976. Thereafter, the heirs of late Tozammel Hussain (i.e. the present appellants) filed an application in the office of respondent No.1 for getting their names mutated in place of Bangladesh Rubber Industries as per their share (i.e. two big has of land in term of the deed of dissolution, vide Annexure-D). The Senior Assistant Secretary (respondent No.3 in writ petition) on the basis of the aforesaid application served notices upon the parties concerned on 6-2-2005 and 20-2-2007 to appear before the Joint Secretary (respondent No.2 in writ petition) with their respective documents. On hearing both the sides, he rejected the prayer for mutation, vide his letter dated 12-6-2007 (Annexure-I) expressing that the Ministry had no scope to interfere with the matter of mutation since a civil suit was pending in this regard but nevertheless directed the parties concerned to inform the Government of the fate of the pending suit or the result of the compromise, if made in the meantime. The further case of the writ-petitioner is that after issuance of letter dated 12-6-2007, the present appellants (respondent Nos.7-9.in writ petition) did not follow the directive of the said notice and beyond the knowledge of present respondent No.1 (petitioner in writ petition) and in collusion with the officials of the Government got the impugned order dated 13-9-2007 (Annexure-J) allowing mutation of their names in respect of two big has of land without serving any notice whatsoever to them and simultaneously communicated the said order to the Assistant Commissioner Land, Tejgaon Circle, Dhaka and other concerned officials for compliance. 

 7. Mr. MI Farooqui, learned Senior Advocate, appearing on behalf of the appellants, submits that the High Court Division committed error of law in construing the deed of dissolution of partnership dated 1-12-1975 (Annexure-D) as a deed of agreement although pursuant to the dissolution of the partnership firm of 1957 the existing partners were entitled to apportion of their respective shares in the form of land, cash money, and the 'good will' of the dissolved firm. After that, some of the partners formed another partnership firm on 9-11-1976 using the name of the firm by virtue of their right in terms of deed of dissolution and would reap the benefit’s of its 'good-will' and got it registered with the Registrar of Firm (Annexure-E). He further submits that by the deed of dissolution (Annexure-D), the partnership registered on 25-5-1957 was dissolved on 31-12- 1975 and the share of the appellants' ancestor, Mr Tozammel Hossain in two bighas of land as per clause-4 of the deed of dissolution of the partner- ship would be moveable property as a result of dissolution under the Partnership Act. Such dissolution would not be required compulsory registration and the Government committed no illegality in mutating the names of the heirs of late Tozammel Hussain in respect of 2 bighas of land. He also submits that the High Court Division committed error of law by giving legal entity to a registered partnership firm because a partnership firm (registered or unregistered) does not come within the meaning of legal person and that in a partnership business, partners carry on business both as principals and as agents for each other within the scope of partnership firm and as such-the impugned judgment should be set aside. 

 8. Mr AM Aminuddin, learned Senior Advocate,appearing on behalf of respondent Nos.1-6, on the other hand, submits that Bangladesh Rubber Industries is a registered Partnership Firm constituted under the provision of Partnership Act, 1932;· As such, it is capable of holding immovable property in its Own name and the immoveable property measuring' 01 acre of land. comprising Industrial' Plot No. 278 of Tejgaon Industrial Area, Dhaka, having been allotted and transferred to the said partnership firm through registered perpetual lease deed, it has become the owner of the said immovable property. As such, to divest the title of the said immoveable property from the partnership firm, a registered deed of transfer, is required and the findings of the High Court Division in this regard is the correct exposition of law and, as such, no interference is called for. He further submits that the deed of dissolution of partnership (Annexure- D) cannot be termed as a deed of dissolution and that if the said deed is construed as a whole .it appears that it is merely an agreement between the parties, Therefore, the High Court Division-rightIy held that the deed of dissolution was, in fact; a deed of agreement among the partners. He also submits that writ-respondent No. 1 with a malafide intention and beyond the knowledge of the respondent-firm issued the letter mutating 2 bighas of land belonging to the respondent firm in the name, of the appellants and, as such, the High Court Division was perfectly justified in declaring the said letter to have been issued without lawful authority. 

 By the deed of dissolution (Annexure-D), the partnership registered on 25-5-1957 was dissolved on 1-12-1975 and the share of the 'appellants" ancestor, 'Mr Tozammel Hossain in two big has of land as per clause-4 of the deed of dissolution of the partnership would be moveable property as a result of dissolution under the Partnership Act and such dissolution would not' be required compulsory registration and the Government committed no illegality in mutating the names of the heirs of late Tozammel Hussain in respect of 2 bighas of land The High Court Division committed, error of law by giving legal entity to a registered partnership firm because a partnership firm (registered or unregistered) does not come within the meaning of 'legal person' and in a partnership business, partners carry on business both as principals and as agents for each other within this scope of partnership business, that the firm's name is a. mere expression, not a legal entity although for convenience it may be used for the sake of suing or being sued, a partnership under the Partnership Act is not a legal person, it is not an entity and it is merely a collective name for the individuals who are the members of the partnership." 

 11. Admittedly, the Government allotted one acre of 'land in the name of the then partnership firm, East Pakistan Rubber Industries by a registered deed of lease executed on 20-11-1970 and registered on 12-2-1971. By a deed of dissolution dated 31-12-1975, the partnership firm formed on 7-5-1957 was dissolved with divisions of assets, good-will etc. among the partners. Soon after dissolution of the earlier firm a new partnership firm in the name of Bangladesh Rubber Industries was formed among the heirs of Noor Hossain as is evident from (Annexure-E), the letter dated 9-11-1976 according registration to the newly created firm. 

 12. Having gone through Annexure-D, the deed of dissolution of partnership, the High Court Division came to a finding that although the heading of Annexure-D and some of its statements manifest that the parties named this deed as the deed of dissolution of partnership, but practically the partnership had not been dissolved and that the same had continued after 'retiring 'of some partners as evident from vital condition No.2 of the said deed. The High Court Division held that Annexure-D, in fact, is an agreement between the existing partners of M/s Bangladesh Rubber Industries in' respect of retirement of particular partners from the partnership firm. The High Court Division came to a finding that clause-4 of Annexure-D stipulated the terms as to the benefit of outgoing partners which manifested that Mr Tozammel Hossain would get two bighas of land from Industrial Plot No. 278 of Tejgaon Industrial Area, Dhaka, owned by the partnership firm while Mr Iqbal Hossain, Mr Sagir Ahmed and Mrs. Zohura Khatoon would be paid in terms of cash for their shares in the properties of the firm and that they would not get any share in the landed property. The High Court Division held that Annexure-B, the deed of lease was registered under the' provision of section 17 of the Registration Act, 1908 since title to the immovable property was to be transferred from the Government of the then East Pakistan to the predecessor of MIs Bangladesh. Rubber Industries by way of perpetual lease. Therefore, the High Court Division held that to divest the said title from the registered partnership firm M/s. Bangladesh Rubber Industries by way of transfer to anybody, a registered instrument was required in accordance with the provision of section 17 of the Registration Act, 1908. The High Court Division observed that when the partnership firm is registered under the provision of section 59 of the Partnership Act, 1932, the acquisition of immovable property in the name of registered partnership firm could not be treated as acquisition by the partners of the firm and that the said immovable property always remained as the property of the registered partnership firm under the provision of section i4 of the Partnership Act,1932. 

 17. Whether a partner's share in a partnership property is treated as moveable property or not, it is necessary to examine the nature of a partnership property. What is important to mention here is that section  a of the (Bangladesh) Partnership Act, 1932, when read along with relevant sections, shows that it is a property which has been originally brought in by the partners when the partnership is formed and also the property which is acquired in the course of business of the firm: There is no gainsaying the fact that as the property belongs exclusively to the firm, no partner can claim any part of the property as his own and what a partner is entitled to is his share of profits only, so long the partnership continues. Upon dissolution of the partnership, his share is his proportion of money representing the firm's asset including immovable property after liquidation of the partnership debts and liabilities. The Partnership Act has been mainly based on English Partnership Act of 1890 and section 22 of that Act referred to 'partnership property' in the following words: , 

 "Where land or any heritable interest therein has' become partnership property, it shall, unless the contrary intention appears be treated as between the partners (including the representatives of a deceased partner), and also as between the heirs of a deceased partner and his executors or administrators, as personal or moveable and not real or heritable estate." 

 18. Commenting thereon Lindley in his partnership stated as follows: "From the principle that a share of a partner is nothing more than his proportion of the partnership assets after they have been turned into money and applied in liquidation of the partnership debts, it necessarily follows that, in equity, a share in a partnership, whether its property consists of land or not, must, as between the real and personal representatives of a deceased partner, be deemed to be personal and not real estate:' 

 24. 'In the case of Commissioner of Income 'Tax, West Bengal, Calcutta vs Juggilal Kamala pat AIR 1967 (SC), 401, the question arose whether non-registration' of the' relinquishment deed invalidates the transfer of the business assets to the new partnership.
